a86.speaker: Anthony Waldhausen, CEO of Msunduzi Association of Residents, Ratepayers and Civics (MARRC)
a86.speech: Explained that the revival of the Bisley RRA came after residents met in November 2024 to oppose construction of a community hall, and said several residents at that meeting volunteered to start the process to revive the association. Said: "The community came together in January this year to protest at the construction site and continued to picket at the site for over three months. It was found that the process for constructing the community hall was irregular and unlawful. It was through the residents' protest that the project was halted and moved to the original site at Oribi Hall." Said MARRC will be available to provide ongoing support and training so the committee can engage their ward councillor and address community issues, adding: "We are finding that residents are mobilising to get organised to address their issues and to hold the municipality accountable."

a86.speaker: Noluthando Mzobe, Chairperson of the Bisley Residents and Ratepayers Association
a86.speech: Said she was honoured and humbled to have been elected chairperson and that this is her opportunity to serve the community: "I look forward to working in collaboration with the team and the community to address the needs of our neighbourhood. Together, I believe we can make meaningful progress and continue building a stronger and better Bisley for all of us." Said her nomination came as a surprise: "I did not realise my neighbours were watching and picking up some positive qualities in me. However, I am goal-driven; I like to see things through. Thus, I feel honoured to be elected as chairperson, and I wish to make the suburb of Bisley proud." Was also proud of how women in leadership are growing: "I am surrounded by a committee of very competent and accomplished men and women, and it's truly exciting that the South African society is at a place where leaders are elected based on their skill and performance rather than gender preference." Expressed her surprise at being nominated for chairperson by men: "To see their confidence in me was also humbling. Also, such experienced men who are husbands and fathers saw a good leader in me due to my passion and organisational skills, and my being a woman was seen as a positive factor."

a130.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Malawi Minister of Youths and Sports
a130.speech: Asked over 1000 TEVETA graduates from Mangochi and Zomba to embrace entrepreneurship in order to create employment for their fellow youths ; said the graduates can reduce unemployment level in the country especially if they start opening up their small scale businesses there by creating self-employment as well as employment for others ; “lt is President Dr Lazarus Chakwera’s version to see that many youths are equipped with technical skills and open up their businesses soon after graduation”.

a130.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Malawi Minister of Youths and Sports
a130.speech: Said that to those without or with small business capital there is a room for them to obtain a loan from National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF) that President Chakwera initiated.

a130.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Malawi Minister of Youths and Sports
a130.speech: Thanked the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) for its financial support of the whole initiative through Titukulane Project: “As government, we want to thank USAID through its Titukulane Project for the initiative because it helped to equip the Youths with different technical skills. And to the graduates, please go and embrace entrepreneurship.”

a130.speaker: Elwin Sichiola, TEVETA executive director
a130.speech: In his remarks, while thanking USAID, said the country needs to have more programs like Titukulane Project.

a281.speaker: Namibian minister (unnamed)
a281.speech: Used the opportunity to encourage exhibitors, highlighting the importance of quality, competitiveness and branding in succeeding on the global stage ; expressed Namibia's readiness to attract foreign investment that can stimulate local industries and create sustainable economic growth.

a302.speaker: Maurice Soudieck Dione, professor of political science
a302.speech: Explains that Mr Sall "felt he needed a certain hold on the political game to protect his rear" in the event of "political score-settling"; also envisages a "personal dimension of non-satiety with regard to power", recalling that Mr Sall had long maintained ambiguity about a third-term candidacy ; "If he had returned, the campaign would have been much more turbulent, bordering on violent. He waged very harsh repression against the opposition. The wounds have not healed."

a302.speaker: Macky Sall, former President of Senegal (five-page letter)
a302.speech: Justified his decision by the need to defend the "gains" of twelve years of presidency and the "dangers" that the economy and democracy would face after less than eight months of "calamitous" governance.

a302.speaker: Ousseynou Ly, spokesman for the Senegalese presidency
a302.speech: Denounced the "indecency" on social media, reproaching the former head of state for the deaths of three years of unrest, the debt and corruption.

a302.speaker: Amadou Moustapha Ndieck Sarre, Senegalese government spokesman
a302.speech: "If he were to return to the country, we would guarantee his security because he is a citizen and a former president of the Republic" ; "But if he came back and the justice system decided to arrest him, neither the Prime Minister nor the head of state could do anything about it."

a302.speaker: Ousmane Sonko, Prime Minister of Senegal
a302.speech: Repeatedly brandishes the spectre of a trial to judge the acts of former leaders and claims to be blocking the departure of former officials; recently spoke of "high treason" in view of the state in which he says he found the public accounts.

a302.speaker: Abdou Mbow, vice-president of the outgoing National Assembly (Sall's camp)
a302.speech: "Rubbish", he exclaims; Mr Sonko "himself knows that he cannot arrest the president."

a302.speaker: El Hadji Mamadou Mbaye, teacher-researcher at the University of Saint-Louis
a302.speech: Doubts that the new regime will go so far as to put Mr Sall on trial, because "at the legal level it will be very complicated" and because Mr Sall has "arrows in his quiver" he could aim at Messrs Faye and Sonko; analyses that Mr Sall is returning to politics because "in reality he never wanted to leave power" and "He feels indispensable", adding that he is not "at the centre of the debate" and that it is Amadou Ba "who has positioned himself as leader of the opposition" ; "I do not think Senegalese are (yet) ready to forgive."

a302.speaker: A Senegalese passenger on a Casablanca-Paris flight (as reported by the press)
a302.speech: Asked Mr Sall, referring to the agitation of recent years: "Why did you kill our children?"

a344.speaker: Ivete Maimbasse, Minister of Land and Environment of Mozambique
a344.speech: Said at the event in Moamba that, in addition to spreading a message of environmental education and combating poaching and trafficking in wildlife products, the panels would promote wildlife and natural landscapes ; "Today, we had the opportunity to witness the unveiling of the double-sided billboard, marking the start of the national initiative promoting biodiversity conservation and nature-based tourism" ; "These panels are vehicles of communication and mechanisms of social mobilization towards a greater individual and collective environmental awareness and for the massification of knowledge about the importance of changing behaviours in relation to the way we look at the biological resources that the country has."

a344.speaker: Mateus Mutemba, director-general of the National Administration of Conservation Areas (ANAC)
a344.speech: Said that the strategy aims to contribute to the awareness of various actors dealing with biodiversity in Mozambique ; "The strategy establishes an audience segmentation of target groups, dividing into groups, namely an internal audience, which is composed of a team from the Ministry of Land and Environment, in general, managers of the conservation areas, employees, management partners from the conservation areas and partners directly involved in the planning and implementation of programs for the protection, conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, constituting all the actors in the implementation of the communication strategy for the conservation of biodiversity."

a344.speaker: Cooperation partners such as USAID and the UNDP
a344.speech: Have promised support for strengthening nature conservation.

a414.speaker: Nabil Abu Rudeina, official spokesman for the Palestinian Presidency
a414.speech: Said that the news circulated by some Israeli media about the so-called establishment of a buffer zone in the northern Gaza Strip and Jabalia to distribute aid to the Gaza Strip through an American private company and with foreign funding is completely rejected and unacceptable, and that such plans violate all resolutions of international legitimacy and international law, which consider the Gaza Strip an integral part of the territory of the occupied State of Palestine.

a414.speaker: Nabil Abu Rudeina, official spokesman for the Palestinian Presidency
a414.speech: Added that all plans related to the future of the Gaza Strip or the distribution of aid there are made only through the State of Palestine and through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) and other international organisations with jurisdiction.

a414.speaker: Nabil Abu Rudeina, official spokesman for the Palestinian Presidency
a414.speech: Pointed out that President Mahmoud Abbas has repeatedly stressed the necessity of implementing UN Resolution No. 2735 immediately, which calls for an immediate halt to the aggression against the Gaza Strip, the urgent entry of aid into the entire Strip, the State of Palestine assuming its full responsibility, and the complete Israeli withdrawal from the Gaza Strip ; he stressed that any temporary plans will not address the roots of the conflict, which will only be resolved by implementing the advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice ending the Israeli occupation and embodying the independence of the State of Palestine with East Jerusalem as its capital.

a414.speaker: Mahmoud Abbas, President of the Palestinian Authority
a414.speech: Has repeatedly stressed the necessity of implementing UN Resolution No. 2735 immediately, which calls for an immediate stop to the aggression against the Gaza Strip, the urgent entry of aid into the whole Strip, the State of Palestine assuming its full responsibility, and the complete Israeli withdrawal from the Gaza Strip.

a414.speaker: Israeli media
a414.speech: Spoke of a plan currently under consideration to establish a buffer zone in the northern Gaza Strip and the Jabalia camp, in order to bring aid into the Gaza Strip through a private American security company with foreign funding.

a591.speaker: United Nations
a591.speech: According to the United Nations, the humanitarian response is facing one of the worst funding crises in decades.

a591.speaker: Director of External Relations, UNHCR (ACNUR)
a591.speech: Recently visited centres hosting Sudanese and South Sudanese refugees in Uganda and warned that more children will die of malnutrition, more girls will be victims of sexual violence and families will be left without shelter or protection, unless the world mobilises, since emergency funding could run out by September.

a605.speaker: David Morewagole, former Alliance for Progressives (AP) candidate in Tswapong North
a605.speech: Feels that the party was not backing them in their fight to contest the constituency under the UDC ticket; he said the rigid stance has forced members to consider going against the party.

a609.speaker: The Presidency of Ghana
a609.speech: Has framed the mass release of 998 prisoners as a humanitarian exercise to decongest overcrowded prisons.

a609.speaker: Evelyn Asamoah, trial judge, Accra Circuit Court
a609.speech: In the case involving evangelist Patricia Asiedua, alias "Agradaa", ordered a pregnancy assessment before sentencing.

a609.speaker: Felix Kwakye Ofosu, Presidential Spokesperson
a609.speech: Who issued the statement, had to come out to deny that the two individuals (William Ato Essien and Agradaa) benefited from the amnesty.

a609.speaker: Prisons Service Council and Council of State
a609.speech: President John Dramani Mahama's decision, announced on Monday, 18 August 2025, followed recommendations from the Prisons Service Council and consultations with the Council of State, in line with Article 72(1) of the 1992 Constitution.

a609.speaker: The Presidency (figures released)
a609.speech: Figures released by the Presidency indicate that 787 of the beneficiaries are first-time offenders; 87 prisoners on death row will have their sentences commuted to life imprisonment, while 51 serving life sentences will have theirs reduced to a fixed term of 20 years; the list also covers 33 prisoners classified as seriously ill, 36 convicts aged over 70, and the two nursing mothers.

a609.speaker: Government of Ghana
a609.speech: Has defended the move as an act of mercy and a pragmatic step towards easing congestion in Ghana's overburdened correctional system.

a758.speaker: United States (official notification to the United Nations)
a758.speech: Asked the United Nations to immediately freeze its contribution to the fund intended to finance the multinational mission supporting the Haitian police in the fight against gangs.

a758.speaker: Stéphane Dujarric, United Nations spokesperson
a758.speech: "We have received an official notification from the United States of the immediate suspension of its (financial) contribution to the multinational security support force," citing this notification as an example of the impact of the general freeze on American international aid announced by Donald Trump; he said that of the $15 million contributed by Washington, $1.7 million had already been spent, indicating that the remaining $13.3 million is now "frozen."

a758.speaker: Lusa news agency (report)
a758.speech: According to Lusa, the MMAS is not a UN force, but the UN created a voluntary fund to finance it which has so far raised $110 million.

a758.speaker: Haitian transitional authorities
a758.speech: Are calling for the mission to be transformed into a UN peacekeeping force.

a758.speaker: United Nations
a758.speech: Announced in early January that more than 5,600 people had been killed by gang violence; according to the UN, gangs now control 85% of the capital, and UN data indicate that more than six million people, almost half the population, need humanitarian aid, more than one million are displaced and about two million suffer severe food insecurity, including 6,000 people in a state of famine.

a758.speaker: UN Human Rights Office
a758.speech: Documented 315 lynchings of gang members and people allegedly associated with them; at least 281 cases of alleged summary executions involved specialised police units.

a952.speaker: NGO Shine Together (statement)
a952.speech: extends its sincere thanks to all the people and organisations that took part in the success of this edition and recalls that its work continues throughout the year in favour of the education, protection and social inclusion of vulnerable children.

a1437.speaker: Idris Elba, British actor
a1437.speech: has told the BBC that he will relocate to Africa within the next decade as part of his plans to support the continent's movie industry ; "I would certainly consider settling down here; not even consider, it's going to happen," he said in an interview on the sidelines of an industry meeting in Accra. ; "I think [I'll move] in the next five, 10 years, God willing. I'm here to bolster the film industry - that is a 10-year process - I won't be able to do that from overseas. I need to be in-country, on the continent." ; "I'm going to live in Accra, I'm going to live in Freetown [Sierra Leone's capital], I'm going to live in Zanzibar. I'm going to try and go where they're telling stories - that's really important."

a1437.speaker: Idris Elba, British actor
a1437.speech: says it is vital that Africans get to tell their own stories; believes that it is vital for Africans to be centre-stage in the entire film-making process ; "This sector is a soft power, not just across Ghana but across Africa." ; "If you watch any film or anything that has got to do with Africa, all you're going to see is trauma, how we were slaves, how we were colonised, how it's just war and when you come to Africa, you will realise that it's not true." ; "So, it's really important that we own those stories of our tradition, of our culture, of our languages, of the differences between one language and another. The world doesn't know that." ; "We have to invest in our story-telling because when you see me, you see a little version of yourself and that encourages us."

a1437.speaker: Idris Elba, British actor
a1437.speech: has previously recognised the talent in Africa's film industry, but said the facilities were "lacking"; believes with the right momentum and involvement of governments willing to create an enabling environment, a virtuous circle can be established.

a1437.speaker: Unesco (2022 report, UN cultural agency)
a1437.speech: said that despite "significant growth in production", the business of film-making across the continent was hindered by issues such as piracy, insubstantial training opportunities and a lack of official film institutions.

a1446.speaker: Maj. Gen. Lul Ruai Koang, SSPDF spokesperson
a1446.speech: told Eye Radio he would respond once authorized to issue an official statement, following reports of the bombardment (non-response).

a1446.speaker: Biel Butros Biel, Commissioner of Fangak County
a1446.speech: reported that two military gunships, a drone, and a fixed-wing aircraft attacked the town around 4 a.m.; according to the commissioner, the strikes targeted the heart of Old Fangak, a town known to shelter tens of thousands of displaced civilians and have no military presence ; "They bombed a civilian centre. They displaced over 30,000 people. The planes belong to the government of South Sudan." ; "We have just gathered information from the town that four people died, including a nine-month-old boy, a very young child, a woman, and two young men. They were all killed in the bombardment." ; "So far, we have confirmed that 25 civilians have been wounded, some of whom are in critical condition and remain in severe health."

a1446.speaker: Biel Butros Biel, Commissioner of Fangak County
a1446.speech: pointed out that the only hospital in Old Fangak, operated by Medecins Sans Frontieres, was also hit in the bombardment and its pharmacy destroyed by fire: "They bombed the hospital... the pharmacy of MSF has been burned to ashes. Some of the wounded are in critical condition, and we don't know how they will survive without medicine."

a1446.speaker: Biel Butros Biel, Commissioner of Fangak County
a1446.speech: condemned the assault, emphasizing that Old Fangak has no connection to any military activities, and called for urgent humanitarian assistance and international attention to prevent further civilian suffering: "We are still gathering information. But what's clear is this was an attack on innocent people, not combatants."

a1446.speaker: Maj. Gen. Lul Ruai Koang, SSPDF spokesperson
a1446.speech: On Friday, May 2, revealed that several barges and boats belonging to a United Nations agency and a Sudanese businessman were hijacked in Leer County, Unity State, and Fangak County, Jonglei State; accused the SPLM-IO and armed youth known as the White Army of being behind the hijacking and issued a warning to the SPLM-IO in the region, warning that Fangak and nearby Leer County would be targeted.

a1446.speaker: Col. Lam Paul Gabriel, SPLA-IO spokesperson
a1446.speech: on Saturday, May 3, dismissed accusations by the SSPDF that their forces detained barges belonging to the United Nations and private businessmen in Adok; in a statement, denied any hijacking or extortion, stating that the boats are docked at Adok port for reasons known only to the businessmen involved.

a1550.speaker: UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel (report)
a1550.speech: Said it had found reasonable grounds to conclude that Israeli authorities and security forces had carried out four of the five genocidal acts defined under international law since the start of the war with Hamas in 2023 - killing members of a group, causing serious bodily and mental harm, deliberately inflicting life-threatening conditions, and preventing births. The report placed responsibility on Israeli civilian and military leaders, cited "explicit statements" by senior officials denigrating Palestinians, and said genocidal intent could be inferred from the scale and nature of Israeli military operations, including the destruction of civilian infrastructure, the imposition of a siege, and the denial of humanitarian assistance. It also examined the "systematic destruction" of healthcare and education facilities, the use of starvation as a weapon of war, sexual and gender-based violence, and the targeting of children, and noted that Israel had disregarded an earlier order by the International Court of Justice. The Commission urged Israel and all states to fulfil their legal obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

a1550.speaker: Navi Pillay, Chair of the Commission and former UN human rights chief
a1550.speech: "The Commission finds that Israel is responsible for the commission of genocide in Gaza" ; "It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria outlined in the Genocide Convention."

a1550.speaker: Navi Pillay, Chair of the Commission and former UN human rights chief
a1550.speech: "The international community cannot stay silent on the genocidal campaign launched by Israel against the Palestinian people in Gaza. When clear signs and evidence of genocide emerge, the absence of action to stop it amounts to complicity." ; Said the evidence showed that responsibility for these atrocities "lies with Israeli authorities at the highest echelons" ; "All States are under a legal obligation to use all means that are reasonably available to them to stop the genocide in Gaza."

a1550.speaker: International Court of Justice (ICJ) order, March 2024
a1550.speech: Instructed Israel to ensure unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza.

a1550.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a1550.speech: According to OCHA, nearly one million people remain trapped in Gaza City amid relentless bombardment, confirmed famine, and "compromised access to means of survival" after Israeli forces placed the entire city under a displacement order.

a1550.speaker: Israel's foreign ministry
a1550.speech: Has rejected the report, describing it as "distorted and false" and politically motivated.

a1550.speaker: Daniel Meron, Israel's ambassador to the UN in Geneva
a1550.speech: Denounced what he called "cherry-picked" findings that promote "a narrative serving Hamas and its supporters in attempting to delegitimise and demonise the state of Israel" ; "The report falsely accuses Israel of genocidal intent, an allegation it cannot substantiate." At a press conference in Geneva he described the inquiry's conclusions as "scandalous" and "fake," accusing its authors of being "Hamas proxies," and said Israel would not cooperate with the commission, which he claimed had a political agenda against the country.

a1550.speaker: Isaac Herzog, Israeli President (reported by Reuters)
a1550.speech: Condemned the findings, saying the inquiry misinterpreted his remarks and ignored the context of Hamas's 7 October 2023 attacks: "While Israel defends its people and seeks the return of hostages, this morally bankrupt Commission obsesses over blaming the Jewish state, whitewashing Hamas's atrocities, and turning victims of one of the worst massacres of modern times into the accused."

a1552.speaker: Pankaj Bedi, CEO of the United Aryan factory
a1552.speech: Said the factory has transformed a once dangerous area of Nairobi, where local gangs would often "steal everything down to the copper cable" when they first set up in 2002: "Today, you can see, it's a well-developed community" ; "We have 150,000 people who directly or indirectly depend on us. It has stabilized the whole socio-economics of the area."

a1552.speaker: Pankaj Bedi, CEO of the United Aryan factory
a1552.speech: On the business's ups and downs: "There were many times when we thought we should give up" ; "But when you have 150,000 people dependent on what you do, you have a responsibility. Shutting down a business is a five-minute job, but to establish and create this kind of platform is not easy."

a1552.speaker: Pankaj Bedi, CEO of the United Aryan factory and participant in the talks as part of the Kenyan Association of Manufacturers
a1552.speech: Remains confident about AGOA's renewal: "I think Trump will be favourable. America cannot produce what we are producing, so he has to find an alternative. Where better than Africa?" ; "Buyers have started to panic. We've been assuring them that it will be okay" ; "Fingers crossed."

a1552.speaker: Norah Nasimiyu, 48, worker representative on the United Aryan shop floor
a1552.speech: "Our families are happy, our children go to school, crime has gone down."

a1552.speaker: Bedassa Tadesse, economics professor at the University of Minnesota Duluth who has studied AGOA
a1552.speech: Said the United States benefits from Africa's cheaper labour, especially in the cost-sensitive clothing sector: "But we have come to this stage where trade policy decisions are no longer just based on cost-benefit analysis." He added that one hope is that Trump will see AGOA as a way of countering Chinese influence in Africa, especially after he axed billions in humanitarian aid.

a1552.speaker: Witney Schneidman, AGOA expert with the Brookings Institution think tank
a1552.speech: Said there was "zero chance" the issue was currently on Trump's radar: "It's small change in Trump's worldview, but it's very important as an instrument in US-African relations, especially when we just lost virtually all our soft power by dismantling USAID."

a1552.speaker: Republicans and Democrats in the US Congress
a1552.speech: Both support an extension of AGOA for at least 12 years, giving companies the long-term security to thrive.

a1603.speaker: The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), United Kingdom-based think tank
a1603.speech: Has warned that President Lazarus Chakwera could face impeachment before his term concludes next year, citing Malawi's severe economic challenges as a key factor ; said the nation's worsening economic situation, characterized by high inflation, rising debt, and widespread poverty, has led to an erosion of confidence in Chakwera's leadership.

a1603.speaker: The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) report
a1603.speech: Highlights several critical economic issues contributing to Malawi's instability, including high inflation, rising national debt and a shortage of foreign currency; points out that dwindling foreign reserves and limited economic growth have deepened Malawi's dependence on foreign aid, making it vulnerable to shifts in donor support; underscores the urgency for the Chakwera administration to implement effective policies to stabilize the economy and restore public confidence as it approaches the end of its term.

a1603.speaker: Political analysts
a1603.speech: Suggest that the impeachment threat is a reflection of growing frustrations with Chakwera's handling of the economy, as well as his government's perceived failure to tackle corruption effectively.

a1603.speaker: Some members of the Malawian opposition
a1603.speech: Have voiced concern that the president has not fulfilled his campaign promises to improve governance and reduce poverty, which have remained significant issues for Malawi.

a1603.speaker: Chakwera's supporters
a1603.speech: Argue that the administration is doing its best to navigate a difficult economic environment and highlight his commitment to structural reforms; they emphasize that many of the issues, including the economic downturn, are influenced by global factors such as the COVID-19 pandemic and other external pressures beyond the government's control; they see impeachment as a divisive distraction that could hinder Malawi's recovery and destabilize governance.

a1603.speaker: Chakwera's administration
a1603.speech: Attributes much of the economic downturn to global factors, including the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and supply chain disruptions.

a1678.speaker: Bassirou Diomaye Faye, President of Senegal
a1678.speech: At the last two cabinet meetings, called "for coherence of interventions and the pooling of resources" of several state agencies.

a1678.speaker: Ousmane Sonko, Prime Minister of Senegal
a1678.speech: Before the deputies on 21 February, announced that by June certain agencies would be merged and others abolished "whose missions can be effectively taken over by central directorates or other non-personalised administrations of the state." ; Sonko also announced a reduction in the salaries of civil servants whose monthly pay exceeds 5 million.

a1678.speaker: Ouest France (newspaper, cited)
a1678.speech: According to Ouest France, nearly 100,000 civil service posts have been eliminated in the United States since January.

a1678.speaker: Le Monde (newspaper, cited)
a1678.speech: Notes that "access to the Oval Office has been opened to influencers, podcasters and figures of the MAGA world."

a1678.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1678.speech: Has always described traditional media as purveyors of fake news; last Thursday he accused the Associated Press of being a "radical left organisation."

a1678.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1678.speech: Stated last Monday, 17 March, on his social network that "the 'pardons' that Sleepy Joe Biden granted to the unelected committee of political thugs, and to many others, are null, void and of no effect."

a1678.speaker: Amadou Ba, Pastef deputy (Senegal)
a1678.speech: Proposes the repeal of the amnesty law voted by Macky Sall's regime before it left power, to be replaced by an interpretative law.

a1754.speaker: Puntland regional state (statement)
a1754.speech: Expressed its gratitude to the United States and the United Arab Emirates for their support in the ongoing military offensive against ISIS militants in the Al-Miskat mountains of the Bari region. In a statement released on Saturday, Puntland acknowledged the airstrikes conducted by the U.S. military and the UAE's involvement, noting their significance in neutralizing key ISIS figures in the region. Puntland also thanked Ethiopia and Kenya for their support during the initial phase of the operation.

a1754.speaker: Pete Hegseth, US Defense Secretary
a1754.speech: Said that the strikes by U.S. Africa Command were directed by Trump and coordinated with Somalia's government.

a1754.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1754.speech: In a post on social media, said a senior IS planner and recruits were targeted in the operation. "The strikes destroyed the caves they live in, and killed many terrorists without, in any way, harming civilians. Our Military has targeted this ISIS Attack Planner for years, but Biden and his cronies wouldn't act quickly enough to get the job done. I did!" ; "The message to ISIS and all others who would attack Americans is that 'WE WILL FIND YOU, AND WE WILL KILL YOU!'" However, Trump did not specify the identity of the targeted ISIS planner or confirm if that individual had been killed.

a1771.speaker: Elon Musk, adviser to the US President
a1771.speech: Tweeted: "USaid is a criminal organisation. Time for it to die."

a1771.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1771.speech: On Monday, Trump alleged, during a meeting with reporters at the White House, that USaid was managed by "radical left lunatics", adding that it was getting away with "tremendous fraud". He did not provide names or details.

a1771.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1771.speech: Told reporters in El Salvador that he was now the acting head of USaid; calling USaid "a completely unresponsive agency", Rubio said a lot of functions of the organisation "are going to continue".

a1771.speaker: Linley Chewere, Director of HIV, STI and Viral Hepatitis in the Ministry of Health (Malawi)
a1771.speech: Said the ministry had redeployed staff for HIV testing, ART dispensing and targeting viral load monitoring to fill gaps left by USaid (PEPFAR)-funded personnel; in a circular, Chiwere said the measures should be implemented without delay as they are part of the contingency plan to respond to the temporary suspension of support by Pepfar and its implementing partners.

a1771.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, economic commentator
a1771.speech: Said the aid cutback represented funding that would otherwise have been covered by Malawian taxpayers: "However, with USaid financing these essential programmes, American taxpayers had been shouldering the cost. The sudden loss of financial support is expected to disrupt development planning and force the government to seek alternative sources of funding."

a1771.speaker: Moses Kunkuyu, Malawi Government spokesperson
a1771.speech: Said developed countries such as the US knew and appreciated that Malawi was one country that had invested heavily in efforts to eradicate poverty, disease and other socio-economic ills but that being a repetitive victim of natural disasters and global economic woes, it was clear that Malawi still needed a hand from the donor community "while we enhance our economic recovery endeavours" ; according to Kunkuyu, the recent resumption of direct budgetary support from some donors was a clear indication that helping Malawi through various programmes was not akin to helping a consuming Malawi but, rather, helping Malawi to stand on her feet ; "It is therefore in the interest of Malawi for rich countries to continue developing suitable partnering arrangements with countries like Malawi as reliable partners in the global development agenda."

a1789.speaker: John Kufuor, former President of Ghana
a1789.speech: Shared insights on democratic transitions and institution-building that provided crucial context for understanding Ghana's development journey; his emphasis on stable institutions as the foundation for sustainable growth resonated deeply with the delegation's HKS studies.

a1789.speaker: Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang, Vice President of Ghana
a1789.speech: Illuminated the new administration's efforts to reform Ghana's economy and strengthen regional integration.

a1789.speaker: Kashim Shettima, Vice President of Nigeria
a1789.speech: Revealed Nigeria's bold policy reforms: "President Tinubu has proven his mettle as a bold and decisive leader," he told them, detailing how the administration tackled the albatross of fuel subsidies; he highlighted initiatives in alternative energy, including a N158 billion investment in electric vehicles for the North-East, and reforms to unify exchange rates and strengthen fiscal policies.

a1789.speaker: Kashim Shettima, Vice President of Nigeria
a1789.speech: Gave a candid discussion of Nigeria's response to foreign aid cuts: "I urged the delegation to look beyond negative narratives and see the real progress we're making," the vice president noted.

a1789.speaker: Olayemi Cardoso, Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria
a1789.speech: Discussed Nigeria's monetary policy reforms, efforts to stabilise the naira, and strategies to control inflation, while promoting economic growth.

a1789.speaker: Aliko Dangote, Nigerian businessman
a1789.speech: "Life is not worth living without ambition. In this life, nothing is impossible," Dangote told the colleagues during a 40-minute Question & Answer session, after personally guiding them through his new oil refinery.

a1789.speaker: Tony Elumelu, chairman of Heirs Holdings, Transcorp, United Bank for Africa (UBA) and the Tony Elumelu Foundation
a1789.speech: Shared his 'Africapitalism' philosophy, emphasising the need for private sector investment to drive economic prosperity in Africa.

a1789.speaker: Babajide Sanwo-Olu, Governor of Lagos State
a1789.speech: Highlighted Lagos as a major hub for finance, technology, and entertainment and engaged the Harvard scholars in a Question & Answer session on his policy efforts and challenges.

a1789.speaker: Management of Tolaram Group
a1789.speech: Shared with the Harvard scholars the company's diversified business portfolio across consumer products, infrastructure, and fintech, with joint ventures like Dufil Prima Foods (Indomie) and Kellogg Tolaram, and investments in infrastructure like the Lagos Free Trade Zone and Lekki Port.

a1789.speaker: A classmate on the policy trek (unnamed)
a1789.speech: Observed about Dangote that his "vision and resilience" serves as "an inspiration to entrepreneurs" globally.

a1805.speaker: US State Department
a1805.speech: Presented the mini-summit as a "targeted" follow-up to the 17th US–Africa Business Summit, held last week in Luanda, where more than 2.5 billion dollars in agreements were signed.

a1805.speaker: Documents cited by Reuters and the Washington Post
a1805.speech: According to these documents, Senegal, Mauritania, Gabon and Liberia — whose leaders are expected in Washington — appear on a list of 25 African countries facing possible migration restrictions, transmitted to African foreign ministries in mid-June, justified by "reliability problems" with identity documents and "administrative fraud".

a1805.speaker: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô, researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a1805.speech: "The presence of these five states, all bordering the Atlantic, reflects the importance the United States attaches to control of coasts that are vital for maritime trade and rich in resources, in a region marked by Russian-Chinese competition" ; he believes that the installation of Russian military bases, arms deliveries via Conakry and military agreements with Togo or São Tomé and Príncipe deeply worry Washington and its NATO allies.

a1805.speaker: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô, researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a1805.speech: Said that Senegal's posture of sovereignty — illustrated by Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko's cancellation of a sports training camp in the United States after a visa refusal, and by the priority given to a visit to Beijing — "cannot leave Washington indifferent".

a1805.speaker: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô, researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a1805.speech: Faced with Trump's unpredictability and a persistent asymmetry, recommends "better African coordination in order to carry more weight in negotiations".

a1805.speaker: Bassirou Diomaye Faye, President of Senegal
a1805.speech: Displays a will for "transparent governance and balanced partnerships" that could complicate American expectations; announced a "technological New Deal" during a tour of Silicon Valley.

a1891.speaker: Hamidou Kadi Yarou, president of the association of women entrepreneurs of Dosso
a1891.speech: Indicated that the women of Dosso have a point of reference in the FSSP president, who enlightened them on the "return to the land", of which she herself is a product with respect to entrepreneurship. It was following the FSSP president's call to say "no to holding out one's hand", she specified, that the women of Dosso decided to support the CNSP within the framework of food sovereignty. This justifies, she stressed, the initiative of the women entrepreneurs of Dosso to develop this groundnut field of more than 20 hectares in order to offset exports that hold back development and empowerment, so as to be a model of agri-food processing, especially in groundnut oil and paste, and so that Niger becomes a reference in this field ; speaking of their association, she indicated that they are organised in associations and it is with the members' contributions that they were able to develop this field, and that the association judged that it can be useful to the country and defend patriotism and sovereignty in agri-food in the Dosso region and thus in Niger, and even export products abroad.

a1891.speaker: Hamidou Kadi Yarou, president of the association of women entrepreneurs of Dosso
a1891.speech: Requested the State's help to further develop their activities.

a1891.speaker: Moussa Brah Raki Djermakoye, president of the Solidarity Fund for the Safeguarding of the Homeland (FSSP)
a1891.speech: Congratulated the dynamic women of Dosso who are working in the processing of groundnuts into oil and paste. "These women," she stressed, "responded to the call of the country's highest authorities regarding the conquest of food sovereignty." ; She stressed that she had met dynamic women who intend to help the country: "They did their best during the patriotic struggle, which earned Mrs Hamidou Kadi Yarou the Saraounia Mangou sovereignty medal," she said, congratulating and encouraging these brave women for all they are doing.

a1891.speaker: Moussa Brah Raki Djermakoye, president of the Solidarity Fund for the Safeguarding of the Homeland (FSSP)
a1891.speech: Assured the women of Dosso that their appeal would be transmitted to the appropriate authorities to help them further pursue the momentum in which they have engaged with regard to food security, and especially the conquest of sovereignty.

a2166.speaker: Robert Mugabe, President of Zimbabwe
a2166.speech: Asserted that South Africa needs help to get full liberation. He said the absence of full liberation explains the xenophobic attacks in the country. He said other Africans should not be blamed for the unemployment problems in South Africa: "It is not the other Africans who are to blame. It is the whites who have kept opportunities for themselves, who have kept the rights they have allocated to themselves long ago before the political dispensation that was brought in by (Nelson) Mandela after his release. That political dispensation did not address the question of disparities between whites and blacks. Most of the land is in the hands of the whites who are a minority." ; He added that most employment opportunities in South Africa are taken up by whites and the topic is never discussed in public forums; he said that this must be addressed before the blame can be allocated to foreigners in South Africa; he said that it is going to be difficult for the South African government to address the issue of unemployment when the same whites who oppressed blacks are still in control of the economy: "When you have people who are in fact those we called oppressors yesterday still in the position, occupying the positions, and the advantages and the opportunities that they had allocated to themselves during colonialism, and they still hang on to them, then you have a difficult situation. This is what South Africa must be helped to overcome." ; "It is a different story in the whole of Africa. So we must help them. They need another liberation." ; said South Africa is the only country in the African continent that is still lagging behind in land redistribution.

a2166.speaker: Robert Mugabe, President of Zimbabwe
a2166.speech: Said he was impressed with the manner in which the SADC secretariat management has given direction to projects agreed upon by leaders of the regional bloc; he was particularly happy with the progress of infrastructure development and regional integration; he said that the programme on transformation of SADC member states' economies is on the right track; Mugabe said the regional body is working on ways to grow the private sector to benefit the citizens.

a2294.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2294.speech: has said the freeze in United States (US) aid has been disruptive to Malawi; according to Chakwera, at the moment, what is important is to seek alternative partnerships to avoid a big sense of loss and let down. He admitted that 27,000 jobs lost was not a small number. ; "A child sometimes grows the same day his father dies. Because now they have a different sense of responsibility they didn't have yesterday. And so, rather than just saying I am finished, you wipe out your tears and make sure that life must go on. So, we will look at other partnerships which could help." ; "In fact, we are discussing [the issue] with them because this new [US] administration will still relate to other nations, including Malawi. And, so, we have always believed in contact and dialogue and we are also doing that even as we speak."

a2294.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2294.speech: "Sometimes, this just shows us that we need to see some things from a distance on how we can be prepared; how to manage some skills by encouraging issues of technology-based programmes, Tevet [technical, entrepreneurial, vocational, education training] programmes - job creation programmes which do not necessarily depend on someone from outside. Because, let's face it, this is truly a global village. You have bilateral relations but you also have multilateral relations and you need to navigate these things." ; He observed that diversifying the economy through the promotion of agriculture mechanisation would help create sustainable jobs. ; "Today's misfortunes could lead to good fortunes tomorrow [prompting us] to look at even the young people we are training now. Are we giving them the sufficient skills matching what is out there on the market so that everyone is relevant?"

a2294.speaker: US Department of State
a2294.speech: The US Government was giving more than $350 million to Malawi annually, according to the US Department of State.

a2531.speaker: German Development Cooperation (GIZ) (press statement)
a2531.speech: In a press statement released by GIZ on Wednesday, November 13, 2024, the dike will improve flood protection for farmland, homes and properties.

a2531.speaker: Rapid needs assessment by GIZ and partner organizations (August)
a2531.speech: This assessment found serious destruction of farms, homes, road infrastructure, drinking water sources and livelihoods ; To protect the remaining farms and reduce future flood impacts, the assessment recommended several measures, including cash transfers, construction and the rehabilitation of dikes.

a2576.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a2576.speech: said on Saturday that a four-year-old child became the second person to die of Ebola in Uganda since the outbreak was announced in late January.

a2576.speaker: Ugandan health officials
a2576.speech: confirmed on Tuesday that the country had recorded 10 infections with the Sudan strain of the virus.

a2576.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a2576.speech: said it and others were working to strengthen contact tracing together with surveillance.

a2842.speaker: Yin (exhibition organiser)
a2842.speech: According to Yin, the fashion show offers a platform for deepening economic partnership between China and Kenya, focusing on trade in high-quality manufactured products and jointly establishing seamless supply chains.

a2842.speaker: Pius Rotich, general manager for investment promotion and business development services at Kenya Investment Authority
a2842.speech: said the government has created a conducive policy and regulatory environment to spur the growth of the textile and apparel sector ; said Kenya is committed to a partnership with Chinese investors in a bid to manufacture high-quality leather products for export in the African market and beyond, boosting foreign exchange earnings and job creation.

a2842.speaker: Gao Wei, managing director of Afripeak Expo Kenya Ltd., co-organizer of the 2025 East African Fashion Show
a2842.speech: said this year's edition had grown bigger in terms of the number of visitors and exhibitors, reaffirming dynamism in the region's textile and apparel sectors ; said the fashion expo will run under the theme of "Inspire Friendship, Connect World," bringing together Chinese and Kenyan enterprises dealing with household accessories, cosmetics, and electronics under one roof ; said the expo will also create a platform for Chinese business executives to network with their Kenyan counterparts, explore two-way trade in leather products.

a2842.speaker: Waceke Mwaura, female entrepreneur
a2842.speech: said that she was impressed by the wig showcased by Chinese exhibitors, adding that its high quality has made it popular among local clients ; said she has been importing hair from China to supply to local retailers and beauty parlors, even as she scouts for distributorship arrangements with Chinese manufacturers.

a2842.speaker: Paul Munyua, a middle-aged pedicurist
a2842.speech: said that he visited the expo to gain insight into new beauty products in the local market imported from China that are affordable to his clients.

a2852.speaker: Local authorities (Tibet Autonomous Region)
a2852.speech: According to local authorities, at least 95 people lost their lives and 130 others were injured in the tragedy.

a2852.speaker: International community
a2852.speech: Quickly offered its support and made offers of humanitarian aid to assist China in its rescue and reconstruction efforts.

a2852.speaker: Chinese authorities
a2852.speech: Have promised to mobilise all necessary means to help the victims and to rebuild the destroyed infrastructure.

a2959.speaker: Godwin Ntadom, Director of Public Health at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (Nigeria)
a2959.speech: Disclosed that approximately 30 million Nigerians are receiving ivermectin treatment for Onchocerciasis (River Blindness) and Lymphatic Filariasis; said that through collective efforts, Nigeria continues to record steady progress in the fight against Onchocerciasis and Lymphatic Filariasis; noted that transmission of Lymphatic Filariasis has been interrupted in 379 LGAs, while the Onchocerciasis Elimination Programme has halted disease transmission in nine states and completely eliminated the disease in two: “About 30 million Nigerians have been weaned off treatment with ivermectin, leading to significant savings and relief for at-risk populations” ; emphasised that with increased efforts, strategic funding, and strong stakeholder collaboration, Nigeria is on track to eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis as a public health problem.

a2959.speaker: Fatai Oyediran, Director and National Coordinator of the NTD Division at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (Nigeria)
a2959.speech: Acknowledged the support of partners such as the Gates Foundation and Sightsavers; reiterated that Nigeria's NTD burden is largely driven by Onchocerciasis and Lymphatic Filariasis: “To date, we have eliminated Onchocerciasis in two states and interrupted transmission in nine others” ; “Additionally, nine more states are in advanced stages of implementation and may interrupt transmission before the end of 2025.”

a2959.speaker: Fatai Oyediran, Director and National Coordinator of the NTD Division at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (Nigeria)
a2959.speech: Identified challenges including drug supply chain issues, lack of diagnostics, funding constraints, and insecurity, while stressing the importance of transparency, accountability, and responsible programme implementation: “There is a need for greater integration and national ownership of the NTD programme.”

a2959.speaker: Fatai Oyediran, Director and National Coordinator of the NTD Division at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (Nigeria)
a2959.speech: Revealed that the programme, initially set to conclude in February 2025, had been extended to September 2025 to allow for thorough impact assessment: “By then, around 32 million people are expected to no longer require treatment under the project.”

a2959.speaker: Anita Gwom, Programme Director at Sightsavers Nigeria
a2959.speech: Highlighted the organisation's more than 20 years of support to endemic communities through medication and preventive care: “We are now focusing on conducting impact assessments and surveys. These are critical to determining whether Nigeria can declare these diseases eliminated. We cannot continue indefinite treatment without proper data” ; called for increased funding, public awareness, and stronger support from state governments and local philanthropists, noting that foreign aid is becoming less reliable: “We urge the Nigerian government and philanthropic community to step up support towards achieving NTD elimination.”

a2959.speaker: Oladele Okogun, Europe-based public health parasitologist
a2959.speech: Expressed optimism: “Though much work remains and challenges persist, the dedication of communities and partners gives us hope. The day will come when no one will need these medicines anymore.”

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Have warned that the shortage of essential medicines in public health facilities was worsening because of prolonged payment delays, contractual uncertainties and a systemic breakdown in the country's medical supply chain; they have since made a series of demands to government including a call for resolving long-outstanding debts from past emergency requisitions, aligning procurement practices with ESPPRA guidelines, especially during emergencies, and publishing clear grading criteria for supplier performance and communicating these during contract implementation.

a2983.speaker: Suppliers' letter of 4 August 2025 to Minister of Health Mduduzi Matsebula
a2983.speech: The suppliers argue that the real problem lies in chronic procurement inefficiencies, regulatory bottlenecks and unpaid invoices dating back months. They say these issues have left them financially exposed and unable to meet urgent orders without formal contracts or payment guarantees. ; "While the minister of finance recently told the nation that all suppliers had been paid in full, this only applies to invoices already submitted to Treasury. In reality, more than E100 million in invoices remain pending at the Central Medical Stores (CMS), with some dating back months."

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Many of these invoices, they say, are unpaid claims which stem from deliveries made under emergency conditions without formal purchase orders, as it happened during a 2023 crisis meeting at Cooper Centre in Mbabane, when suppliers were urged to provide goods against requisitions. Some of those requisitions, the suppliers allege, were never converted into official orders, leaving them with no payment and no recourse.

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Suppliers counter that partial fulfilment can result from global shortages of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), manufacturer minimum order requirements or minor production losses, all beyond their control. They add that government rarely adheres to the agreed 45-day payment period, while late payments to suppliers are not penalised in the same way late deliveries are.

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Suppliers complained that the shift to framework contracts had introduced significant uncertainty because the ministry of health does not commit to minimum purchase quantities or clear delivery timelines. This uncertainty, they claim, undermines their ability to negotiate competitive prices with manufacturers, secure financial backing from lenders and plan stock procurement effectively. ; "Manufacturers will not give best pricing without guaranteed minimum orders. Without such commitments, they may cancel or refuse to process our orders when they finally come."

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Suppliers also cite repeated delays in finalising contracts, stating that tenders are typically released in late November or early December, a period when many global manufacturers are on shutdown, with bids due in early February. They say government deliberations then stretch for four to five months, leaving a gap of several months without valid contracts after the financial year ends on 31 March. ; "This year, the award schedules for Tender 2 (Pharmaceuticals and Vaccines) were only received in early June, and urgent orders were placed soon after, yet formal contracts had still not been signed by the end of July, despite some deliveries already having been made."

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: The suppliers made it known that they raised strong objections to being asked to urgently airlift stock from overseas and fast-track deliveries without signed contracts in place, warning that delivering under such conditions leaves them with no legal recourse for payment. They also point to discrepancies between tender documents and contract terms, particularly in delivery lead times, which could expose suppliers to penalties for delays beyond their control. Further, they claim that suppliers are graded on past performance without being told the criteria, while government delays in paying invoices are not factored into those assessments.

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: They cite confusion over the respective mandates of the MRU and the long-anticipated Medicines Regulatory Authority (MRA), no formal appeals process for rejected submissions and the absence of a single reference document outlining MRU guidelines and procedures. According to the suppliers, MRU staff sometimes lack the training to verify compliance documents issued by overseas manufacturers and are unwilling to liaise with regulatory counterparts in exporting countries to resolve disputes. Suppliers also called for MRU representation on the tender board to avoid awarding contracts for products that are later rejected at the listing stage.

a2983.speaker: Local pharmaceutical and medical suppliers (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: They informed the minister that importation hurdles are another major concern as import permits are said to be reviewed only once a week, delaying procurement cycles and international payments, as banks require the permits to process transfers. They also cite the financial strain of having to pay import taxes upfront on zero-rated goods, with VAT refunds often delayed for months. The suppliers recommend digitising the permit process, increasing permit review frequency to at least twice weekly, clarifying MRU and MRA roles, and fast-tracking the formal establishment of the MRA as required under the Medicines and Related Substances Control Act of 2016. They have formally requested a response from the ministry of health within 10 days and expressed their readiness to engage at any time.

a2983.speaker: Ministry of Health (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Has repeatedly insisted that poor performance by suppliers is at the root of drug shortages; in recent weeks, the ministry issued urgent requests to suppliers to fast-track deliveries, including airlifting certain orders from overseas in a bid to address stock gaps. The ministry has reportedly argued that partial deliveries indicate a lack of supplier capacity.

a2983.speaker: Neal Rijkenberg, Minister of Finance (Eswatini)
a2983.speech: Recently told the nation that all suppliers had been paid in full.

a2983.speaker: Sources (anonymous)
a2983.speech: According to sources yesterday, the ministry had yet to reply, despite the letter being sent on Monday.

a3157.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of Namibia
a3157.speech: Acknowledged those who played pivotal roles in organising the women’s conference in Beijing; highlighted her advocacy for gender equality, stating that society should not downplay the role of any group, especially women, in shaping the social, political, and economic landscape; highlighted the Swapo Party’s bold decision to adopt a 50/50 representation policy in leadership roles; while acknowledging that global gender equality is still a work in progress, she noted that Namibia has made significant strides, though more remains to be done ; “I believe that having been elected as President of my country will encourage women from all walks of life to stand up to be counted, with a clear understanding that I was not elected because I am a woman, but on merit. That is to say, as women, we should not ask to be elected to positions of responsibility because we are women, but because we are capable members of our societies to hold those positions.”

a3157.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of Namibia
a3157.speech: Laid out a clear agenda for Namibia’s future, focussing on tackling unemployment, improving education, and promoting sustainable economic development; aims to strengthen Namibia’s global standing through economic partnerships and regional cooperation; believes a green revolution is possible with Namibia’s resources, boosting agriculture to meet food needs and supply raw materials for manufacturing and thus driving industrialisation and job creation ; “The diversification of our economy will generate additional revenue to finance development and to enhance and expand social safety nets. It will also create jobs to take care of the unemployed, the majority of whom are the youth. Opportunities will be created for the effective participation of the youth in the various sectors of our economy through targeted financing; training, mentorship and internship programmes. As part of the youth empowerment programme, the government will promote the various sports codes and invest in appropriate infrastructures to enable our sportsmen and women to compete effectively in the international arena. Attention will also be given to the creative industry to make space for our people to bring out their talents.”

a3157.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of Namibia
a3157.speech: Reaffirmed Namibia’s commitment to deepening regional integration through SADC and the AU, particularly through the African Continental Free Trade Area.

a3157.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of Namibia
a3157.speech: Reaffirmed Namibia’s support for peaceful conflict resolutions and the rights of Palestine and Western Sahara to self-determination, and called for the lifting of sanctions against Cuba, Venezuela, and Zimbabwe.

a3157.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of Namibia
a3157.speech: Reflected on the legacy of the late Founding President, Dr. Sam Nujoma, and all the leaders who played a significant role in Namibia’s liberation, acknowledging their contributions that paved the way for her inauguration.

a3219.speaker: An economic operator (businessman, anonymous)
a3219.speech: “Who, then, has an interest in investing in a country where people want to kill the Head of State?”, one economic operator remarks ironically.

a3219.speaker: Concordant sources (anonymous)
a3219.speech: According to concordant sources, this American development financing agency (USAID) is reportedly about to turn its mission into a mere liaison office, with the consequence of a drastic reduction in the aid envelope for Benin.

a3290.speaker: Nur, Somali (former) minister
a3290.speech: Told Anadolu Agency (AA) on Wednesday that the visit upgraded relations to a strategic dimension. He stated that Somalia was in a state of collapse and was experiencing one of the worst droughts before Erdoğan’s visit: “In those days, Somalia was cut off from the world and left without aid. When President Erdoğan visited Somalia with his Cabinet and family, it marked a significant turning point for the world. It wasn’t only the assistance of the Turkish people, but global attention also turned to Somalia (thanks to his visit).” ; Emphasizing that Türkiye has never distanced itself from Somalia since Erdoğan’s visit, Nur said: “Since that day, we have continuously progressed. Türkiye has played a major role in the reconstruction of Somalia.” Nur added that Türkiye has always stood by Somalia in its fight against terrorism, in its development efforts and in improving the welfare of its people. He mentioned that Türkiye-Somalia relations began with humanitarian aid but have now progressed to a strategic level, noting that cooperation is underway in major sectors, including oil, fisheries and even space exploration. Nur stressed that Türkiye’s presence in Somalia brings joy not only to the Somali people but also to all friendly nations. Recalling his time in Türkiye in 2011 as both a student and a second secretary at Somalia’s diplomatic mission there, Nur said he could never forget those days: “The Turkish people have always stood with the oppressed and continue to do so. If the Somali people have come through those dark days to where we are now, Türkiye, President Erdoğan and the Turkish people have played a significant role in that.”

a3290.speaker: Mohamed Dhuubow, director of the Somali Investment Promotion Office at the Ministry of Planning, Investment and Economic Development
a3290.speech: Commented on Erdoğan’s visits: “The 2011 visit was for humanitarian assistance, but the second visit in 2016 was a development mission.” Dhuubow stated that Türkiye’s role in Somalia has extended into investment and infrastructure. “Significant developments have taken place in Türkiye-Somalia relations. Turkish Airlines launched flights to Mogadishu, followed by Turkish companies operating at the port and airport, which transformed Somalia’s economy. Today, numerous Turkish investors are active in sectors ranging from banking to construction,” he said. He noted that Somalia’s new company law allows foreign investors to own property and that Turkish businesspeople have taken a pioneering role in this process.

a3290.speaker: Ali al-Sadiq, former Foreign Minister of Sudan
a3290.speech: Told AA that Türkiye topped the list of countries that may play a key role in the reconstruction of Sudan, which is gripped by strife. “Türkiye stood by Sudan and supported displaced refugees,” he said on Wednesday. He emphasized that Africa has long been seen as an area of economic exploitation by Western countries: “The time has come for African nations to take control of their destinies and determine their futures themselves.” Praising Türkiye’s support to many African nations, he said they expect Türkiye to expand its influence further across the continent, and that this outreach should include almost every African country, many of which need aid, expertise and higher education.

a3290.speaker: Ali al-Sadiq, former Foreign Minister of Sudan
a3290.speech: Expressed Sudan’s desire to expand cooperation with Türkiye, stating that Sudan possesses vast resources in agriculture, water, mining and livestock. He especially noted the potential benefits of Türkiye’s expertise and technology in agriculture and expressed appreciation for the opening of a Ziraat Katılım Bank branch in Port Sudan at a time when millions of Sudanese have been displaced. Al-Sadiq called for the development of mechanisms to enhance Turkish-Sudanese cooperation, emphasizing the need to establish a transportation corridor between the two countries. He said that peace has been restored in nearly three-quarters of Sudan and that now is the time to begin strategic cooperation between the two countries.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Thanked the "honourable members for the contributions to the debate on the State of the Nation Address", saying he especially welcomes the contributions on economic growth, and that the proposals put forward, as well as the criticisms, are taken seriously.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said the debate saw the expression of divergent views, also among parties making up the GNU, and that it is expected that the 10 parties do not always agree: "The GNU is working well together, whether people like it or not." ; said the GNU demonstrated it can put its political differences aside and work for the common good and is committed to upholding our "hard-won democracy."

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said some MPs held firm to the denialism their parties require from them and that those who said "vacuous things" like no progress is being made knew that they were "talking to the wind"; said this is not conducive to nation-building in a diverse country and underlines the importance of the upcoming national dialogue.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said several MPs spoke about the land question, which he previously described as the "original sin" in South Africa, and that the 1913 Native Land Act plunged millions of South Africans into poverty and its impact endures today; said the process of restitution is not complete.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Spoke of the forced removal of District Six: "There are some in this house today who have memories of their families being forcibly removed from their land." ; "That is why we will never allow forced removals again in this country," saying that is why we have a Constitution prohibiting arbitrary removals.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: "We will not be diverted from the path we have set out. And I would like to repeat, we will also not be bullied by anyone, in the country or outside." ; "We must not allow others to divine us, but more importantly, to divide us," saying we are facing a "harsh global wind" and it is not the time for any of us "to rush off to a foreign land" to complain about things we can sort out ourselves.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said the structural reforms initiated under Operation Vulindlela are well under way: "We will move with even greater urgency and determination to ensure that these changes, these reforms, are implemented." ; "We are introducing competition and dynamism," saying it is key to creating jobs ; "There is a determination to be innovative, to be creative."

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said Parliament is a "reservoir of wisdom" and we should be proud that we are a democracy that approves laws and not the "arbitrary whims of a ruler", adding that he must assent to bills passed by Parliament if the bill is constitutional and cannot halt it based on agreements between parties.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said the challenges in the logistics system are being resolved and markets for South Africa's products are being expanded: "We have skills, and we have experience and know-how that we need to harness, not only to expand existing industries but also to grow new industries." ; said the WEF ranked SA as the leading tourism destination on the continent last year, and talked about the green economy and digital economy.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: "The infrastructure drive is gaining momentum," saying public sector infrastructure is on the rise for the second consecutive year and existing infrastructure must be maintained; applauded the premiers for what they are doing in the provinces and said infrastructure is the flywheel of the economy.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said that for investment to grow there must be a "razor sharp focus" on local governance: "Strong municipalities are needed to achieve strong local economies." ; said government must continue working with traditional leaders and that there is growing collaboration between traditional leaders and local government entities.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Welcomed the suggestions and proposals put forward on education: "Our children must have a strong literacy and numeracy base, from the earliest phase," agreeing that technical and vocational training needs to be strengthened; said we must work to dispel the notion that self-employment is only for those who can't be absorbed by the formal economy.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Said that despite severe financial constraints government continues to provide pro-poor policies and that they want a society that takes care of those in need.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: "What is clear in this debate is that we all want a country that is transformed," saying there is consensus across the political spectrum on non-racialism; said they will ensure the Transformation Fund achieves its objectives and told those opposed to it to sit back and think through how the government will foster transformation: "These policies are about eradicating the differences that still exist in our society, not entrenching them," adding it is about empowering those who have been disempowered.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: Welcomed the debate about SA's participation in the DRC: "The decision to deploy our armed forces is not taken lightly. Particularly when it places our armed forces in harm's way." ; said direct negotiations and dialogue among state parties and non-state parties, including M23, must resume, and that South Africa will do whatever is in our means to ensure peace in the DRC.

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a3422.speech: "I am convinced that despite our differences, we share a common desire for a South Africa that belongs to all who live in it." ; concluded: "Let us all unite to take this country forward, and work hard for the people who elected us here."

a3422.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa (SONA)
a3422.speech: Announced plans to invest R940 billion in infrastructure over the next three years and secure R100 billion in financing from local and international institutions, setting out plans to drive economic growth, create jobs and invest in infrastructure.

a3422.speaker: Bheke Radebe, House chairperson
a3422.speech: Said several rules have been violated towards the end of the debate - members of the public participated and MPs didn't sit while he spoke; earlier ruled that all other members were audible and that a ruling had been made and Trollip could write to the relevant office.

a3422.speaker: Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, Electricity Minister
a3422.speech: Said Hlophe attributed the successes between 2009 and 2018 to an individual and blamed the challenges on an organisation, and that this is duplicitous; said GDP growth between 3.5% and 5% will be achieved but it would be folly for Ramaphosa to declare 5% would be achieved by the end of the term; said Macpherson's relationship with the truth is hostile and the infrastructure agenda was generated during the Sixth Administration; concluded "We will go and explain ourselves to the allies" and "We will not be bullied."

a3422.speaker: Mzwanele Manyi, MKP chief whip
a3422.speech: Said it is a serious understatement to say that SONA was an anticlimax and that Ramaphosa is not serious about transformation; said all the targets for the National Development Plan have been missed; said the MKP is a government in waiting, "ready to take over yesterday", and will not govern through lies and deceit; "We see you," he said to the government, adding people are struggling with load reduction in the townships, maybe not in the suburbs, "where the neo-liberals live"; said the Expropriation Act is not a progressive act and will delay land reform, and that MKP will table a private members bill for expropriation without compensation and will ensure parliamentary sovereignty so the courts cannot overturn parliamentary decisions.

a3422.speaker: Baxolile Nodada, DA deputy chief whip
a3422.speech: Said the DA joined the GNU because they couldn't risk the EFF and MKP gaining power, who would have tanked the economy; said the DA will help to grow the economy and create jobs; said he strongly believes the DA can bring changes to the NHI to ensure universal healthcare and that what gives them stomach aches is the failing public health system; said just today it was revealed Lesufi's government stole over R600 000.

a3422.speaker: Sihle Lonzi, EFF MP
a3422.speech: Said Chairman Mao popularised the concept of a paper tiger and that Ramaphosa's state of the nation address, like the seven before it, is a paper tiger; said the EFF felt the pain of deputy minister of public works and infrastructure Sihle Zikalala because Ramaphosa reduced him to the "boy of an illiterate matriculant white man".

a3422.speaker: Marlon Daniels, PA MP
a3422.speech: Said the PA is excited by the prospects of 3% growth announced by Ramaphosa and that the country will be turned into a construction site as it will create jobs; "Let job opportunities rain from our African sky!" ; said he wants the transformation fund to be a "rainbow nation project" to benefit all people.

a3422.speaker: Wonderboy Mahlatsi, UAT leader
a3422.speech: Questioned whether those who ran to America to complain about expropriation are truly Africans - "Where is honourable McKenzie's slogan now? Abahambe!" ; said the land question is not only about history but about survival and that if South Africa reaches a boiling point it will not be about political debate, it will be about land; called on Ramaphosa to implement expropriation without compensation.

a3422.speaker: Tammy Breedt, FF Plus MP from the NCOP
a3422.speech: Said Afrikaners have no other home than South Africa and they'll help to build the country; said seven months ago, during the opening of Parliament, she asked that municipalities should be prioritised, and that this SONA was the first time Ramaphosa acknowledged the challenges, thanking him for listening to GNU partners.

a3422.speaker: Bridget Masango, DA MP
a3422.speech: Said Ramaphosa's SONA was different and inspired hope, not because he said anything new but because of the GNU ministers and deputy ministers, and that some of the programmes he referred to came right out of the DA's election manifesto; said the DA wants to grow the economy and lift the 28 million SASSA grant beneficiaries out of State dependence; said the alternative to the GNU is "terrifying"; welcomed Ramaphosa's inclusion of people with disabilities in the economy.

a3422.speaker: Panyaza Lesufi, Gauteng Premier
a3422.speech: Thanked Ramaphosa, saying that during last year's SONA debate he asked him to sign the BELA Bill and, like a "true listening president", he has signed it, opening the doors to learning and culture, and that opponents have threatened him with legal steps but so far "dololo" (nothing), because you can't take non-racialism to court; thanked him for signing the NHI Act: "No one can challenge equity and access to quality healthcare for everyone."

a3422.speaker: Panyaza Lesufi, Gauteng Premier
