a7492.speech: On the World Bank debt report: said the increase in costs shifted scarce resources away from critical needs such as health, education, and the environment in developing countries; “We are worried that the record debt levels and high interest rates have set many countries on a path to crisis while every quarter that interest rates stay high results in more developing countries becoming distressed and facing the difficult choice of servicing their public debts or investing in public health, education, and infrastructure.” He said the situation warrants quick and coordinated action by debtor governments, private and official creditors, and multilateral financial institutions, with more transparency, better debt sustainability tools, and swifter restructuring arrangements, as the alternative is another lost decade.

a7492.speaker: Dr. Tony Okpanachi, Managing Director/CEO, Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN)
a7492.speech: On high interest rates: said surging interest rates have intensified debt vulnerabilities in all developing countries, with 18 sovereign defaults in 10 developing countries in the past three years alone — more than in all of the previous two decades; that about 60 percent of low-income countries are at high risk of debt distress or already in it; that most of these countries face the additional burden of accumulated principal, interest and fees incurred under the G-20’s Debt Service Suspension Initiative (DSSI); that the stronger US dollar is adding to their difficulties; that new external loan commitments dropped by 23% to $371 billion in 2022, the lowest level in a decade; that private creditors received $185 billion more in principal repayments than they disbursed in loans; and that the World Bank and other multilateral development banks stepped in, providing $115 billion in new low-cost financing in 2022, with the World Bank providing $16.9 billion more through IDA than it received in principal repayments and disbursing $6.1 billion in grants.

a7492.speaker: Dr. Tony Okpanachi, Managing Director/CEO, Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN)
a7492.speech: On MSME financing in Nigeria: said MSMEs are collectively the largest employers in many low-income countries including Nigeria, yet their viability is being threatened by lack of access to risk-management tools such as savings, insurance and credit; noted the exclusion rate reduced from 53 per cent in 2008 to 46.3 per cent in 2010, that the Central Bank of Nigeria launched the National Financial Inclusion Strategy on 23rd October 2012 aimed at reducing the exclusion rate to 20% by 2020, and that DBN was conceived by the Federal Government in collaboration with the World Bank, African Development Bank, German Development Bank (KfW), French Agency for Development and European Investment Bank, obtaining its Wholesale Development Banking licence in March 2017.

a7492.speaker: Dr. Tony Okpanachi, Managing Director/CEO, Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN)
a7492.speech: On sector focus: said DBN is not status specific, but over time will encourage some growth sectors in line with the development objective; “The key thing for us is that whatever sector of the economy you are, the questions are, are you able to create employment? Are you able to empower people? And all these things will help in diversification of the economy, which are the developmental impact you want to make in the economy.”

a7492.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF) World Economic Outlook
a7492.speech: Said inflation was coming down and acute stress in the banking sector had receded, but the balance of risks facing the global economy remained tilted to the downside and credit was tight; projected global real GDP growth of 3.0% in 2023, up 0.2 percentage point from its April forecast, and left its 2024 outlook unchanged at 3.0%; indicated new technologies could boost productivity but could be disruptive to labor markets; described the outlook as “broadly stable” in emerging market and developing economies for 2023-2024, with growth of 4.0% in 2023 and 4.1% in 2024; noted credit availability is tight and there was a risk that debt distress could spread to a wider group of economies, and that the impact of higher interest rates was especially evident in poorer countries, driving debt costs higher and limiting room for priority investments.

a7492.speaker: Dr. Tony Okpanachi, Managing Director/CEO, Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN)
a7492.speech: On development finance in Africa: said development finance of Africa has its limitations in amounts available, acceptable repayment risk and in some cases financing cost vs project viability, and that such finance often comes with strictures on how African nations should run their economies, so that solutions that are imported rather than developed at home may inadvertently come at a hefty price; said there is no denying that the traditional development finance model has not worked for Africa over the past six decades, that most African nations turn to development aid to survive, which is not a viable model to achieve sustainable economic development, and that since 1990 African countries have received over $1.3 trillion in development assistance while the continent’s financial, societal, and political fabric remains fragile.

a7511.speaker: Ghana National Chamber of Pharmacy (GNCoP) and Pharmaceutical Importers and Wholesalers Association (PIWA) (joint statement)
a7511.speech: Announced that prices of pharmaceutical products have been reduced by 5 to 15 per cent across the board: "However, in support of government efforts to stabilise the economy and reduce inflation, and in the interest of the public health and consumer welfare, GNCoP in consultation with PIWA have resolved to reduce their prices by 5-15 per cent across the board. This decision is a demonstration of our sector's commitment to national development and public health."

a7511.speaker: Ghana National Chamber of Pharmacy (GNCoP) and Pharmaceutical Importers and Wholesalers Association (PIWA) (joint statement)
a7511.speech: Commended the government for the recent measures that have led to a marked and sustained appreciation of the cedi against major foreign currencies, particularly the US dollar, and said the cedi's appreciation has provided relief to the pharmaceutical sector: "It said a stronger cedi means lower foreign exchange costs for pharmaceutical importers, resulting in lower prices for essential medicines and health products." ; Explained that currency stability allowed for better forecasting, planning, and pricing, particularly important for small and medium pharmaceutical enterprises, and added that with reduced cost pressures, pharmacies and hospitals were now better positioned to stock essential medicines.

a7511.speaker: Ghana National Chamber of Pharmacy (GNCoP) and Pharmaceutical Importers and Wholesalers Association (PIWA) (joint statement)
a7511.speech: Said "while we acknowledge these recent gains, it is important to note that the sector has, over the period absorbed a huge percentage of the cost due to the depreciation of the cedi", and that many businesses were holding old stocks procured at higher rates, with the financial burden on importers and distributors remaining considerable.

a7511.speaker: Ghana National Chamber of Pharmacy (GNCoP) and Pharmaceutical Importers and Wholesalers Association (PIWA) (joint statement)
a7511.speech: Said government must continue its prudent economic management and maintain support for the private sector, especially the pharmaceutical industry: "We remain hopeful that this stability will be sustained in the long term. The Chamber & PIWA also reiterate its commitment to working collaboratively with the government and all stakeholders to ensure the pharmaceutical sector remains vibrant, accessible, and sustainable for the benefit of all Ghanaians."
